claims.claim: At 40 requests/s and a mean insurer call of about 400 ms, bookings alone keep roughly 16 of 17 sync workers busy at peak
claims.why: This is Little's-law arithmetic on the team's own figures; the benchmark has no 400 ms upstream wait and no 17-worker setup to check it against.

claims.claim: If the insurer goes from 400 ms to 2 s, capacity drops about 5x and every endpoint stalls
claims.why: The benchmark measured only one upstream wait (10 ms), so it cannot show how sync-worker capacity changes as the wait grows.

claims.claim: gevent doesn't help cancellations much, because cancellation is mostly a database state change rather than a long wait
claims.measured: One-row DB query: gevent 1,905 req/s vs sync 1,529 (gthread 2,119); 20 queries: gevent 369 vs sync 441. In contrast, 10 ms I/O wait: gevent 2,956 vs sync 276
claims.why: On database work gevent was within about 1.25x of sync Flask and sometimes slower; its big gain (about 10x) appeared only in the I/O-wait test.

claims.claim: Adding sync workers or containers costs more per request than gevent
claims.measured: I/O wait: sync 276 req/s at 122 MB peak vs gevent 2,956 req/s at 67 MB; idle memory 115 MB vs 60 MB
claims.why: Sync Flask used more memory and handled far fewer waiting requests than gevent, so it does cost more per request when requests wait on I/O.
